newsitem.title: Australia: Australia announces good jobs data, analysts wary.
newsitem.headline: Australia announces good jobs data, analysts wary.

text.p: Australian employment data released on Thursday showed a second sucessive strong monthly rise in jobs and the lowest unemployment rate in five months, but analysts remain concerned about the jobs market.
Official data showed employment rose 24,400 in November, an unexpectedly strong rise considering it followed October's 25,500 rise.
The unemployment rate came in at 8.5 percent, its lowest level since July, and well down on October's 8.8 percent.
Despite the jobs data coming in on the strong side of expectations, economists said it was too early to claim that the worst of the labour market slowdown had passed.
"I don't think it tells us that it's the start of the acceleration in employment growth," SBC Australian senior economist Guy Bruten said.
"We probably won't see any sort of acceleration in employment growth until we get to the second quarter of next year," Bruten said.

Employment weakness has been one of the major concerns of economic policymakers this year, and it has been a key factor behind the three interest rate cuts delivered by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) since July -- the most recent being the half point reduction to 6.0 percent announced on Wednesday.

"The combination of a cut in interest rates and better than expected employment figures on the eve of Christmas will boost consumer confidence," Prime Minister John Howard told parliament on Thursday.

But despite the apparent strength seen in the last two months -- where total employment has risen by almost 50,000 -- economists said there was still a way to go before the jobs market recovered from the weakness seen in 1996.
"While there are some signs of strength returning to the labour market, the overall picture is of a labour market that is still soft," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said.
Over the first 11 months of the year, employment has risen by only 61,600, hardly a sign of robust growth, while the unemployment rate is above the 8.1 percent of last December.

"The best interpretation (of the data) is still that the jobless rate has been moving sideways for more than a year and a half, and that no quick change to this state can be expected," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.
Also adding to economists caution was the fact that most of the recent jobs growth has been in part-time employment.

Westpac senior economist John Peters said that as most of the growth in November employment, and in employment throughout 1996, had been in part-time jobs, "it doesn't really alter our view that labour market conditions are pretty weak".
Part-time jobs are seen as having less flow through effects on spending because they normally pay less than full-time jobs.
Economists also said that when companies start lifting full-time employment it is a sign of increasing confidence in the economy.
Signs of definite recovery in the jobs market should become apparent around mid-1997, when the impact of the three interest rate cuts will start to spur on the economy, analysts said.

"The economy, and the labour market, are not in free fall and the raft of rate cuts over the past five months have set the scene for a stronger 1997," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
